newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Gazprom flexes muscle in Central Asia.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Gazprom flexes muscle in Central Asia.

text.p: Russia's Gazprom gas company, a corporate empire which fears it may one day be challenged by the energy-rich former Soviet republics, said on Thursday it would assert control over the flow of gas from Central Asia.
Gazprom chief executive Rem Vyakhirev said the world's largest gas company would not let Kazakhstan export gas through Russian pipelines, which Gazprom controls.

He also told a news conference Gazprom would create a venture with Turkmenistan to export that country's gas -- but he spoke only of sales to cash-poor customers in the former Soviet republics, and not of exports to Europe.

The move angered Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov, who suggested he had been locked into a deal which would keep his state, which could sit on the world's fourth-largest estimated reserves, out of export markets controlled by Gazprom.

"Yesterday in talks with (Prime Minister) Viktor Stepanovich (Chernomyrdin) and with Rem Vyakhirev, I felt the smell of old Soviet ambitions, when they said, OK, we can do without your gas," Niyazov told a separate news conference.
But Vyakhirev said: "We and Turkmenbashi (Niyazov) were and remain friends -- I often go there as a guest. He added later: "I don't know of any markets from which Turkmenistan has been crowded out."
Vyakhirev's visits are probably more for business than for pleasure, since Turkmenistan is part of two large planned pipelines that could cut into Gazprom's gas supplies to Europe.

The sparks from the two energy powerhouses come after the United States said last month it would not oppose plans to build a $1.6 billion pipeline to carry Turkmen gas across Iran to Turkey and eventually on to Europe.
Gazprom, the world's largest gas producer, meets 60 percent of Europe's gas import needs and sits on 34.5 percent of the world's gas reserves.

But the company is under pressure on two fronts. Russia's former Soviet neighbours, whose gas industries Gazprom controlled when it was a ministry, are seeking to sell their own gas to the West and to Asia.

And Russia's cabinet reformists want more competition in Russia's domestic gas industry, in which Gazprom is a monopoly which accounts for nearly all of gas output and completely controls the transport of supplies both at home and abroad.

Gazprom's new venture with Turkmenistan to export Turkmen gas replaces an earlier arrangement which flopped. Vyakhirev did not say whether Turkmenistan could sell gas to Europe via the new venture, using Russian pipelines.
In a separate challenge to Gazprom, Turkmenistan also hopes to export much larger volumes through a proposed pipeline that would link Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan.
"We've heard about how much they could export to Pakistan -- we will continue to work on this theme," Vyakhirev said, adding Gazprom would also carry out unidentified work in Iran.
He also made it clear that Russia was not keen to see competitive supplies from Kazakhstan, another former Soviet republic in Central Asia.

"Under no circumstances will Kazakhstan export gas through Russia," Vyakhirev said, when asked about the giant Karachaganak gas field, which is being developed by Texaco Inc, British Gas, Agip and Russia's LUKoil, and which once included Gazprom as a partner.
"To give up one's market...would be, at the very least, a crime before Russia," he said.
Gazprom has said it aims to increase five-fold its supplies to Turkey by 2005 to 30 billion cubic metres, or bcm, a year. The Turkmen-Iran line would have a capacity of up to five bcm.
The new venture Vyakhirev announced replaces one which allowed Turkmenistan to export 20 bcm of gas to Europe annually in addition to supply CIS customers, notoriously bad payers.
Niyazov dissolved the old agreement in March, reportedly over displeasure with Gazprom's stranglehold on Turkmenistan's access to Russian-controlled export pipelines.
The move trashed Turkmenistan's gas-dependent economy, which saw industrial output dive over one-third in the first half.
